SESSION 1 · THE PIXEL

You see a cat. A camera records numbers.

The image has meaning to us; to a computer, it begins as a grid.

Human: “That’s a cat.”
A DIGITAL IMAGE
451 × 300

This photograph is stored as 135,300 pixels.

Each color pixel has three numbers: red, green, and blue.

Computer vision turns pixels into useful information.

A pixel stores color. It does not come with a little label that says “ear”, “whisker”, or “cat.”

SESSION 1 · FROM RULES TO LEARNING

Rules are easy to write. Good rules are hard.

Imagine describing a cat to a computer using only “if” statements.

HAND-WRITTEN RULES
if pointy_ears and
  whiskers:
  return “cat”

But what about a dog with pointy ears? A cat seen from behind?

Easy case
Same cat, a harder view
Machine learning takes another approach: learn useful patterns from examples.

SESSION 1 · NEURAL NETWORKS

What lives inside a neural network?

Small calculations connect to other small calculations.

THE BASIC IDEA

Lots of adjustable connections

Each connection has a weight: a number that controls how strongly one signal matters.

After training, the weights help turn an input into a prediction.

Training changes the weights, not the rules written by a person.

SESSION 1 · RECAP

Session 1: three things to remember

We now have the pieces of a learning system.

01

Images are numbers.

Pixels are the raw material of computer vision.

02

Models learn from examples.

Labels tell us which answers we want.

03

Training changes the model.

The goal is useful predictions on new examples.

SESSION 2 · GENERALIZATION

Try changing the lighting.

Would you still recognize the cat? Move the slider.

GENERALIZATION

Old object, new conditions.

When a model performs well on situations beyond its training examples, we call that generalization.

Light, background, distance, and viewpoint can all change what the pixels look like.

SESSION 2 · SHORTCUTS

Why would a model take a shortcut?

It follows patterns in its data—even patterns we did not intend.

Object

Background

Another background

Two kinds of pattern

Useful: the shape and appearance of the object.

Misleading: a background that happens to appear with the same label again and again.

A model can give the right answer for the wrong reason.
Photos/textures: scikit-image Chelsea, grass, brick · Teaching comparison

SESSION 2 · IMPROVING DATA

What would you change in the training examples?

We can change the data before changing the model.

DATASET A

One background per shape

Shape and background are linked.

DATASET B

Both shapes on both backgrounds

Background alone no longer predicts shape.

If our goal is to recognize shape, which dataset offers better examples?

SESSION 2 · RESEARCH THINKING

One strange prediction is a research clue.

A failure is useful when we can ask what changed.

Clear photo
Dark + blurry
THINK LIKE A RESEARCHER

Observation

Imagine a model that works on clear images, but struggles on dark and blurry ones.

Possible explanation

It relies on small visual details that disappear in poor lighting.

What could we try?

More varied examples, a different image representation, or a better model.

SESSION 2 · RESEARCH THINKING

Research turns “what if” into evidence.

A small investigation follows a repeatable cycle.

01

Notice

What is going wrong?

02

Explain

What might cause it?

03

Test

Change one thing.

04

Compare

Did it improve?

Research is not only building a model. It is finding questions and checking ideas carefully.
Teaching diagram of the hypothesis–experiment–evaluation cycle
27 / 31
SESSION 2 · FROM 2D TO 3D

A photograph shows only one side.

We can recognize the object—but what do we know about what we cannot see?

ONE VIEW OF AN OBJECT

The front can look identical for two different 3D objects.

What is behind it?

One picture cannot show every hidden surface.

We may need more viewpoints—or a model that makes an informed guess.

If the front looks the same, can the back be different?
Interactive geometry illustration · One visible view is insufficient to fix hidden surfaces
28 / 31
SESSION 2 · FROM 2D TO 3D

Turn the object around.

Choose two different backs. The front view stays the same.

AN AMBIGUITY

Different 3D worlds can make the same 2D picture.

A camera captures what is visible from its viewpoint. The missing side remains unknown.

Recovering shape from images is a central challenge in 3D computer vision.

One image is evidence—not the entire object.
Rotating block: self-contained 3D projection illustration
29 / 31
SESSION 2 · THE BIG PICTURE

From recognizing things to understanding a scene.

Computer vision keeps asking harder questions about the same world.

RECOGNITION

What is it?

Cat, car, cup, person.

GEOMETRY

Where is it?

Location, size, distance.

3D UNDERSTANDING

What shape is it?

Surface, hidden parts, possible motion.

Photo: scikit-image Chelsea · Detection box and 3D cube: illustrations
30 / 31
SESSION 2 · CLOSING

Two sessions. One bigger question.

We have moved from pixels to learning—and from learning to research.

WHAT WE NOW KNOW

Pixels are numbers in a grid.

Learning connects examples to predictions.

Testing tells us whether patterns carry over.

Research asks why and tries something new.

ONE QUESTION TO KEEP

How much can a computer learn about the 3D world from pictures?

This is where our next conversations can begin.

2D images→3D shape→Motion
